rv.q: Majok, a Tony nominee and Pulitzer Prize-winner for her play “Cost of Living,” skillfully weaves together the women’s experiences of desperation, grief and survival.
"Queens," directed with a sensitive hand by Trip Cullman, is more loosely constructed (and prolix) than some of Ms. Majok’s plays, reflecting the scattered nature of its characters’ experiences.
The play overall celebrates, movingly and unabashedly, the fortitude behind it.
Majok’s expansive work lives up to their talents, and allows each of them to shine, capturing two moments (2001 and 2017) at an overcrowded basement apartment in the titular New York borough.
Queens is a sprawling portrait of immigrant women's experiences made energetic and compelling by a phenomenal cast.
The overall effect of powerfully detailing the immigrant experience is achieved.
Ireland’s performance bores through the crowd like a laser beam.
These interludes are powerful, but so stylistically different from the rest of the play as to feel jarring.
And yet, as strong as its message is, and as well acted, there are structural problems with the play that undermine its full power.
Queens is excellently acted and directed (by Trip Cullman), but for much of the running time, it's downright confusing.
Its empathy for such people is palpable, but its muddled storytelling, indefinite characters, awkward language, and excessive length make it dramatically unappealing.
It is a beautifully acted, sharply cut, deeply felt production.
This specific production of 'queens' is not to be missed.
I highly recommend a trip to the basement of New York City Center to witness this powerful journey.
Martyna Majok’s Queens turns a cramped Queens basement into a stage for American ambition, powered by Marin Ireland and an ensemble that refuses to beg for your pity.
The ensemble’s commitment alone brings authenticity and depth, making the play a worthwhile experience.
Still, Queens captures an essential quality of lives lived in the margins with performances that are simply astonishing.

cn.t: Majok's timely immigrant drama earns praise for its powerful ensemble cast and emotional resonance, though some critics find it overcrowded and muddled. Strong performances elevate this affecting portrait of marginalized women in a Queens basement.

vr.q: Rounded out by some thoughtful and impactful design elements, this is a great production.
